title: Acute‐onset chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy with cranial nerves and respiratory tract involvement: A case report
case_prompt:
A 59-year-old man, previously healthy, presented with progressive ascending paresthesia and weakness beginning 10 days after a flu-like illness. Within 24 hours he developed paresthesia in his upper limbs, and by day 2 he had weakness of the lower and then upper limbs, along with discrete dysphagia and frequent choking on liquids. He was admitted on day 8 of symptoms. Three days into hospitalization he developed respiratory weakness and worsening dysphagia; by day 14 he had facial diplegia. No autonomic dysfunction was noted. 

On examination, he had flaccid tetraplegia (MRC grade 3/5 in the upper limbs and 2/5 in the lower limbs), absent reflexes, glove-and-stocking hypoesthesia, a positive Romberg sign, and facial diplegia. Nerve conduction studies showed sensory and motor demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with decreased motor conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies in the ulnar, median, tibial, and peroneal nerves, prolonged F-wave latencies in all four limbs, and decreased sensory conduction velocities in the right musculocutaneous and left ulnar nerves. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed albumino-cytologic dissociation with 0 white cells and protein 0.7 mg/dL.

He was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome and received a single course of IV immunoglobulin, with progressive improvement; at discharge his strength was MRC 4+ and respiratory and bulbar signs had resolved. Two weeks later, he returned with worsening dysphagia and new sensory ataxia. Examination showed positive Romberg sign, loss of deep sensation on the right, absent reflexes, MRC grade 4+ strength, a weak gag reflex, and mild facial diplegia. He was treated with a second course of IV immunoglobulin, resulting in complete resolution of dysphagia and ataxia. After discharge he continued to improve, recovering all reflexes, with only mild proximal weakness and paresthesia treated with pregabalin.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) — “The patient was initially diagnosed as GBS and received an immunoglobulin therapy.”  
2. Recognition of treatment-related fluctuation of GBS — “This was considered as a treatment‐related fluctuations (TRF), and the patient received a second immunoglobulin therapy with a complete regression of the dysphagia and the sensory ataxia.”  
3. Consideration of acute-onset chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (A-CIDP) — “up to 16% of CIDP patients may present acutely like AIDP the demyelinating form of GBS, developing in <8 weeks and a subsequent chronic progression sharing similar clinical and electrophysiological findings.”
